transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
President Trump says the U.S. should only be selling China older chips in the wake of
intensified scrutiny of Nvidia, the world's top supplier of high-end chips used for AI.
You have to understand China makes chips, too.
And if we're not going to sell them, they'll make them themselves.
That's one of the reasons that Jensen would use, used to try and say, like, hey, and he
was, he's a good man.
By the way, he's a man while we're at it.
He made some bad decisions.
Trump defending Nvidia's former CEO, Jensen Huang, who recently resigned after reports
of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
The president was addressing reporters about his first trilateral meeting yesterday with
the presidents of China, Xi Jinping, and of Russia, Vladimir Putin.
Trump said he and China agreed on joint guardrails for AI.
And Trump also expressed warm sentiments for Putin.
Former U.S. ambassador to Russia, Michael McFall, had this reaction to that.
I don't think he understands what it means to represent the United States of America
when he goes abroad.
And he kind of said it himself.
Caitlin Collins asked him about, you know, what you're doing for America.
And he said, well, I don't, I think he meant I don't speak for America or maybe, but I
think he said I don't speak to America.
But Putin is my friend.
McFall on NPR's Here and Now.
The House Ethics Committee is trying to change the way it handles sexual misconduct investigations.
Here's NPR's Elena Moore.
The panel approved the internal rule changes on Thursday by a unanimous vote.
It comes after the committee announced earlier in the week it was reviewing several rule
changes, including one that would give the chair or ranking member subpoena power without
needing a full committee vote.
Another focused on, quote, consolidating deadlines for when a member who's being investigated
has to respond to findings.
These steps come after multiple House lawmakers faced high profile sexual harassment and misconduct
allegations this year.
And the committee weathered criticism for moving too slowly on investigating cases.
Elena Moore, NPR News.
The federal appeals court has temporarily suspended the permit for the army's planned detonation
of roughly five tons of unstable lead-base explosives in southeast Iowa.
Here's Iowa Public Radio's Tom Barton.
The court put the EPA's emergency permit on hold late Thursday while it considers a request
to block the blast at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown.
Two Iowa environmental groups say the EPA didn't fully consider safer options.
They say toxic lead dust could travel 100 miles or more depending on the weather.
Federal officials say they've been planning since March and are prepared to take extensive
precautions to protect the public.
After Iowa and Illinois lawmakers called for a delay, the army postponed the blast to Monday.
It says detonating the 68 drums where they're stored inside earth-covered concrete bunkers
surrounded by sand-filled barriers and water misters poses the lowest risk to the public.
For NPR News, I'm Tom Barton in Des Moines.
This is NPR News.
The Iraqi government has reached a deal with a major Iran-backed militia over control of
bases near Baghdad.
NPR's Jana Raff reports the move diffuses fears over clashes between militia fighters
and Iraqi security forces.
Iraqi security officials announced Friday that government forces would deploy to Jervon Nasser
where Iran-backed Qatab Hezbollah has bases.
The government has accused the paramilitary group and some government officials of oil-smuggling
operations in the area south of Baghdad.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zadeh has pledged to disarm Iraq's extensive network of armed
groups that aren't fully under government control.
While some have agreed, Qatab Hezbollah, one of the most powerful, has refused to give
up its weapons.
Jana Raff, NPR News, Amman.
New psychedelic treatments could become more widely available as soon as next year.
Here's NPR's Will Stowe.
Studies on psychedelics screen patients carefully beforehand and monitor them closely while
they're under the influence.
However, a minority of patients do experience new and sometimes serious difficulties in
the weeks and months after.
Research suggests serious adverse events like suicidality are very rare in drug trials.
Experts like Roman Politsky at Emory University School of Medicine, who's running a study
on this, says it isn't being tracked well enough and the full array of problems aren't
being documented.
"Quite common on the list are things like anxiety, depression."
Others are existential distress, insomnia, and feeling disassociated.
Will Stone, NPR News.
